schema.name: SuggestSkills
schema.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

keywords.description: Topic keywords from the user's request.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. ## cityflo-ontime
Answers 'which routes were actually late this week, by how much, and which three were worst'. Start with methodology and data_quality_report, then route_verdicts and worst_routes; drill into route_detail / trips for evidence. Defaults are the committed decision rules (SPEC.md); parameters exist only for what-if replay. Datasets are named folders under the configured data root.

## plugin:dodopayments:dodopayments-api

  This is the dodo payments MCP server.

  Available tools:
  - search_docs: Search SDK documentation to find the right methods and parameters.
  - execute: Run TypeScript code against a pre-authenticated SDK client. Define an async run(client) function.

  Workflow:
  - If unsure about the API, call search_docs first.
  - Write complete solutions in a single execute call when possible. For large datasets, use API filters to narrow results or paginate within a single execute block.
  - If execute returns an error, read the error and fix your code rather than retrying the same approach.
  - Variables do not persist between execute calls. Return or log all data you need.
  - Individual HTTP requests to the API have a 30-second timeout. If a request times out, try a smaller query or add filters.
  - Code execution has a total timeout of approximately 5 minutes. If your code times out, simplify it or break it into smaller steps.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__data_quality_report
entries.description: Every excluded or flagged row by rule and trip id, dropped columns, and REC-114 4xx identifiability.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__incidents
entries.description:
Incident route-days (median lateness > threshold) with affected trips and rider impact (D9/D11), plus any
    dated incident context from incidents.csv. Ops-log entries are NOT joined (undated); see ops_log.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__list_datasets
entries.description: List the datasets available under the configured data root, and which one is the default.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__methodology
entries.description: The committed decision rules (D1-D11) with their default parameters. Read this first.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__ops_log
entries.description: Ops-log entries as weekday/time/category (D6). Complaint lines are category-only; all text is redacted.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__rec114_impact
entries.description:
REC-114 shown separately (D2): identifiable 4xx trips, the primary view, and counterfactual views as if the
    whole route ran on the revised flat runtime (from effective date / all week), plus lateness by runtime band.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__rider_impact
entries.description:
Rider-impact view (D11), kept separate from the systematic ranking: trips >5 late, excess minutes beyond
    tolerance, and how much of each route's impact sits on incident days.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__route_detail
entries.description:
Everything behind one route's call: metrics, verdict with/without incident days, rank and stability,
    per-day breakdown, lateness by scheduled-runtime band, exclusions and REC-114 status.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__route_verdicts
entries.description:
One verdict per route (D8, all valid trips) plus its D9 character with frequency, magnitude (median/p85/p95), day consistency,
    incident days and exclusion counts. Non-default parameters are a what-if, not the committed answer.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__trips
entries.description:
Trip-level drill-down. Filters: route, date (YYYY-MM-DD), status ('valid', 'excluded', or a reason code),
    min_lateness (minutes), flag (e.g. tz_corrected). Sorted by scheduled departure. Shows the raw and normalised
    timestamps and the runtime actually used, so any number can be recomputed by hand.

entries.name: mcp__cityflo-ontime__worst_routes
entries.description:
Ranked worst-N (D10): late_share desc, median desc, route asc. Includes day-bootstrap rank stability
    (P in top-N, P same rank) and the next routes below the cut so the boundary can be challenged.

{
  "default_params": {
    "tolerance_min": 5.0,
    "late_share": 0.3,
    "min_median": 3.0,
    "incident_day_median_min": 15.0,
    "min_trips": 20,
    "extreme_abs_min": 120.0
  },
  "lateness (D1)": "arrival (normalised to IST) - (scheduled_departure + applicable runtime), minutes",
  "applicable runtime (D2)": "export scheduled_runtime_min, except REC-114 revised runtime for trips that are IDENTIFIABLY 4xx (vehicle_series/vehicle_class exactly 4NN) on/after effective_date",
  "exclusions (D3,D4)": "unparseable timestamps (e.g. 08:60), invalid runtime, invalid OR MISSING tz_offset ([impl] conservative: assuming IST would be an unsupported repair), arrival not after scheduled departure. Each is reported by trip id; none is repaired.",
  "timezone (D5)": "arrival converted from its stamped offset to +05:30 and kept",
  "late trip (D7)": "lateness > tolerance_min (5)",
  "route verdict (D8)": "LATE iff late_share >= 0.30 AND median >= +3, on all valid trips",
  "incident days (D9)": "[impl] route-day with median lateness > 15 min (an analytical implementation choice, not an assignment requirement). Incidents are NEVER removed from the D8 verdict; instead each LATE route is characterised: systematic (no incident days), mixed (D8 still passes without incident days), incident_driven (D8 passes only because of incident days). NOT LATE routes with an incident day are marked incident_day_only. Incident trips stay in rider-impact totals",
  "worst-N (D10)": "sort by late_share desc, median desc, route code asc; stability from a seeded day-level bootstrap (1000 draws)",
  "rider impact (D11)": "trips_late and excess_minutes = sum(max(0, lateness-5)), reported separately",
  "ops log (D6)": "Context only (D6): entries carry a weekday but no date, so they cannot be reliably joined to route-days (for the week-2026-08-03 bundle, HANDOFF calls it LAST week's log, while DATA_GUIDE says 'from the week'). Never used to exclude, adjust or excuse a trip; dated incidents belong in incidents.csv."
}

## 1. Route verdicts (`route_verdicts`)
Five routes are **LATE**, and all five are `systematic`: none has an incident day.

| Route | Verdict | Character | Valid trips | >5 min late | Late share | Median | p95 | Days passing the rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R-14 | LATE | systematic | 118 | 85 | 72.0% | +8 | 16 | 7/7 |

| R-31 | LATE | systematic | 112 | 37 | 33.0% | +4 | 9 | 4/7 |
| R-17 | NOT LATE | — | 147 | 41 | 27.9% | +3 | 10 | 2/7 |
| R-35 | NOT LATE | incident_day_only | 132 | 32 | 24.2% | +2 | 54.5 | 1/7 |

The other 33 routes are NOT LATE. Each has a late share of 22.6% or less and a median of +3 or less. The tool flags R-26, R-37, R-31 and R-17 as borderline.

## 2. Worst three (`worst_routes`)
| Rank | Route | Late share | Median | Bootstrap: chance of being in top 3 | Bootstrap: chance of the same rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | R-14 | 72.0% | +8 | 1.00 | 0.998 |
| 2 | R-33 | 47.1% | +5 | 0.94 | 0.70 |
| 3 | R-26 | 42.7% | +4 | 0.66 | 0.45 |
| *4* | *R-37* | *40.0%* | *+4* | *0.29* | — |
| *5* | *R-31* | *33.0%* | *+4* | *0.04* | — |

The tool returned no warnings. R-14 and R-33 are solid picks. The third slot is not.

## 3. R-26 vs R-37 (`route_detail`)
- **Rule says R-26:** its late share is 42.7% against 40.0%, with the same median of +4. That's a gap of about 3 trips.
- **Evidence leaning toward R-37:**
  - It's more consistent day to day: 6/7 days pass the rule, against 5/7 for R-26.
  - It has slightly more trips over 10 minutes late: 5 against 4.
  - It has no excluded rows; R-26 has 2.
- **Rider impact** is about the same: 131 against 125 excess minutes.
- **Bootstrap** keeps R-26 in the top three in 66% of draws and R-37 in 29%.

R-26 is ranked third by D10, but in the decision record it should be called a close call over R-37, not a clear pick.

## 4. R-31 vs R-17: the LATE line
- **R-31 is LATE with a small margin.** 37 of 112 trips are late (33.0%), and 34 is the minimum to pass. 3 fewer late trips would flip it. Its median is +4, it passes the rule on only 4/7 days, and none of its trips is more than 10 minutes late.
- **R-17 is NOT LATE because of the share test alone.** 41 of 147 trips are late (27.9%), so it is 4 trips short of 30%. Its median of +3 passes, but only just.
- **R-17 has more rider impact than R-31:**
  - 41 late trips against 37
  - 130 excess minutes against 91
  - 7 trips more than 10 minutes late against 0

  It still fails the rule on 5/7 days.

The verdict follows D8 as written, and I haven't tuned anything. The point to make in the write-up is that both routes sit within a few trips of the threshold.

## 5. R-35: incident vs systematic (`route_detail`, `incidents`)
- **Wednesday 2026-08-05:** all 19 of 19 trips were late. The median was +52 minutes, with a minimum of +36 and a maximum of +61.
- **That one day accounts for 880 of the route's 914 excess minutes (96%).** 914 is the highest rider impact on the network; R-14 has 416.
- **The other six days are clean.** Without the Wednesday, 11.5% of trips are late and the median is +1. Every other day fails the rule.
- **The primary verdict (all trips) is NOT LATE,** marked `incident_day_only`. The incident still has to appear in the weekly answer, as D9 requires.
- **There's no dated cause.** No `incidents.csv` exists, and the undated ops log is not joined to trips (D6).

## 6. REC-114 (`rec114_impact`, `data_quality_report`)
**No trips are identifiable as 4xx.** The `vehicle_series` column holds only the last two digits, so the primary verdict applies the revised runtime to 0 trips (D2).

The tool also computes two counterfactuals, which never feed the verdict:
- **Revised from the effective date (2026-08-05):** the whole route runs on the revised flat runtime from that date.
- **Revised all week:** the whole route runs on it for the full week.

|---|---|---|---|
| R-14 (revised to 53 min) | 72.0% late, +8, LATE | 43.2%, +4, still LATE | 31.4%, +0, **NOT LATE** |

- **5,292 rows:** 5,250 valid and 42 excluded.

content.text:
The adversarial review turned up a bigger risk than the one you flagged. **R-26 vs R-37 holds up better than it looks. The real threat to the answer is REC-114.** If a reviewer insists the revised runtime applies to all of R-14 and R-27, R-14 drops from #1 to #3, or out of LATE altogether, and R-27 enters the top three.

All figures come from the MCP tools. Where I did arithmetic on their outputs (z-tests, worst-case bounds, counterfactual re-ranking), I've said so. Nothing has been modified.

## 1. R-26 vs R-37

**What late-trip share means for the business.** It's the chance that a rider on a randomly chosen scheduled trip arrives more than 5 minutes late: how often the route can't be trusted. It's weighted by trip, not by rider, because we have no ridership data. Median lateness then sets a floor on how late "late" usually is.

**Should 2.7 points outweigh day consistency?** Not as a matter of statistics. A two-proportion test on the tool's counts (44/103 vs 42/105) gives z ≈ 0.39, p ≈ 0.7, and that's generous because trips on the same day aren't independent. On late share alone the two routes are tied, and the rule breaks the tie deterministically. But the "6/7 vs 5/7 days" argument is weaker than it looks:
- **Head to head by day,** R-26 has the higher late share on 5 days (Mon, Wed, Thu, Sat, Sun). R-37 is higher on 1 (Fri), and Tue is tied.
- **R-37's extra passing days are fragile.** It passes on Sat and Sun at exactly 33.3% (5 of 15 trips), so one trip either way flips each day. A pass/fail count over 15-trip days is noisier than the weekly share.
- **R-26 is equal or worse on almost every magnitude measure:**
  - mean +4.51 vs +4.13
  - excess minutes 131 vs 125
  - late minutes 482 vs 474
  - identical median, p85 and p95

  The only exception is trips over 10 minutes late: 4 vs 5, a single trip.
- **R-26 is much worse in the evening peak:** 55.6% late at +7 on 27 trips, against 26.9% at +3. R-37's worst time bands are before 07:00 and after 20:00, with only 10–11 trips each. That suggests more riders are affected on R-26, but without ridership data it can only be supporting evidence.

**Would a reasonable reviewer reject R-26 at #3?** They can argue it's a tie. They can't show R-37 is worse. On nearly every measure R-26 is equal or worse. R-26 also keeps #3 at a 3-minute tolerance, at every share threshold from 25% to 35%, at median floors of 2 to 4, and under the data-quality worst case (section 5).

**Proposed wording:**
> **#3 R-26: a close call over R-37.** Both are systematically late with a median of +4. R-26 is late on 43% of trips against 40%, worse on 5 of 7 days head to head, and twice as late-prone in the evening peak (56% vs 27%). The gap is about 3 trips, which is not statistically meaningful. We rank R-26 third under the pre-committed rule, and treat R-26 and R-37 as joint third for operational follow-up.

**What would make us switch to R-37:**
- 3 of R-26's late trips are shown to be data errors.
- Ridership weights show R-37's late trips carry more riders.
- A 4xx mapping changes either route's runtimes.
- Cityflo explicitly redefines "worst" as severe (>10 min) lateness. That's a different question, covered in section 6.

The excluded rows can't cause a switch; section 5 shows the bound.

## 2. R-31 vs R-17
R-17 has the larger total impact because it runs **31% more trips** (147 vs 112). Totals grow with how much service a route runs. Per trip, the two routes are almost the same: 0.88 vs 0.81 excess minutes (my arithmetic).

They differ in shape:
- **R-31** runs a steady, modest delay: median +4, no trips over 10 minutes.
- **R-17's** lateness is lumpy:
  - Friday alone is 52% late; the other days range from 14% to 33%.
  - 7 trips run more than 10 minutes late.

**Feature or flaw?** Mostly a feature. D8 is meant to flag routes that are *routinely* late, which is a timetable or operations problem, and keep total harm in the separate rider-impact view (D11). R-17 is the second-highest rider impact among NOT LATE routes, behind R-35. The real weakness is the hard cutoff:
- R-31 passes by 3 trips and drops out at a 35% threshold.
- R-17 misses by 4 trips and becomes LATE at 25% or at a 3-minute tolerance.

I see no compelling methodological reason to change D8. Changing it after seeing the results would be tuning. **Recommendation:** label both routes **marginal** in the memo, with their trip margins, and list R-17 in the rider-impact watch list.

## 3. R-35
Four lenses give four different answers:

| Lens | Answer for R-35 |
|---|---|
| Rider experience this week | **Bad.** Wednesday was the worst route-day on the network. R-35's weekly mean (+8.05) is effectively tied with R-14's (+8.07). |
| Systematic route lateness (D8, Wednesday included) | **NOT LATE.** 24% of trips late, median +2. The other six days are on time: 11.5% late, median +1. |
| Incident-driven | **Yes.** On Wed 5 Aug, 19/19 trips were late, by +36 to +61 minutes. |
| Rider impact (D11) | **Highest on the network:** 914 excess minutes, 2.2× R-14. 880 of those minutes fall on Wednesday. |

A reviewer will notice that a mean-based ranking would put R-35 at #2. The memo has to say this openly: we deliberately use share and median to answer "is this route chronically late", and report the incident in its own right.

**Proposed wording:**
> **R-35: not late as a route, but the week's worst single disruption.** On Wednesday 5 August every one of R-35's 19 trips ran 36–61 minutes late (median +52). That's 880 rider-minutes beyond tolerance, more than double R-14's whole week. Wednesday is included in R-35's verdict, not removed. The route is NOT LATE because the other six days ran on time (11.5% of trips late, median +1), so this looks like a one-day disruption, not a timetable problem. The cause is not established: no dated incident record was supplied, and the ops log is undated. R-35 needs an incident review and rider remediation for Wednesday, separate from the chronic-lateness list.

The memo should say "disruption", not "incident", unless a cause is confirmed. "Incident day" is our label for the pattern only.

## 4. REC-114
**Your reasoning is defensible.** The exact handoff wording helps: "trips on the 4xx vehicle series are measured against the *revised* timetable … so the numbers line up with what the review already has". The handoff also says "Apply them as you see fit."

Three points make it stronger:
1. **The field can't identify the series.** DATA_GUIDE defines `vehicle_series` as the "last two digits of the vehicle class". In every trip I sampled, the series equals the route number: R-14 → "14", R-27 → "27", and all 70 R-26 trips I pulled → "26". So the column looks aligned to routes, not vehicles. It can't tell 114 from 414.
2. **Applying it to the whole route contradicts the timetable file.** `schedule_v2` marks R-27 "no change". Yet a flat 45-minute runtime applied to all of R-27 would turn it from NOT LATE (22%) into LATE (43–47%) and put it in the top three. A "no change" route jumping into the worst three is strong evidence that route-wide application is not what was signed off.
3. **The directive is implemented.** The rule runs automatically on any trip whose class is identifiably 4NN. The memo should say: *"REC-114 is applied to every trip the data identifies as 4xx; this week's export identifies none."* It should not say *"we did not apply REC-114."*

The handling has two weak points we must face head-on:
- **The impact is large, so it can't go in a footnote.** My re-ranking of the tool's counterfactual shares:
  - Revised from 5 Aug: worst three become **R-33, R-27, R-14**.
  - Revised all week: R-14 becomes NOT LATE, and the worst three become **R-33, R-27, R-26**.
- **The stated purpose is to match the review's existing numbers.** If the review applied REC-114 route-wide, our R-14 figures won't match theirs. The counterfactual table is the reconciliation, and it needs to be in the memo itself.

## 5. Data quality: worst-case bound
I took each route's excluded count from the tools and recomputed the share twice: once with every excluded row treated as extremely late, and once with every row treated as on time.

| Route | Excluded | Late share, as reported | Range under both extremes |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-14 | 1 | 72.0% | 71.4–72.3% |
| R-33 | 1 | 47.1% | 46.7–47.6% |
| R-26 | 2 | 42.7% | 41.9–43.8% |
| R-37 | 0 | 40.0% | 40.0% (fixed) |
| R-31 | 0 | 33.0% | fixed |
| R-17 | 0 | 27.9% | fixed |
| R-35 | 1 | 24.2% | up to 24.8% |
| R-27 | 4 (network max) | 22.4% | up to 24.5% |

- **R-26 stays above R-37 in every case.** Its lowest possible share (41.9%) is still above R-37's 40.0%.
- **R-26's median stays at +4 or more.** 63 of its 103 valid trips are 4+ minutes late (from the `trips` drill-down), which holds even with 2 on-time rows added.
- **No verdict can flip either way.** The highest NOT LATE share possible is 27.9%. The LATE routes nearest the line have no exclusions.

So the defence is: *42 rows (0.8%) were excluded. Even if every one were counted as extremely late, or as on time, no verdict and no worst-three position would change.* The evidence that they're artifacts is supporting detail:
- All 24 bad timestamps read exactly `08:60`, whatever the scheduled time.
- All 18 pre-departure rows are exactly 5 minutes early.

## 6. Threshold sensitivity
All of these are what-if runs (`what_if: true`). Only the defaults are the committed answer.

| Tolerance / share / median floor | LATE routes | Worst three | P(R-26 in top 3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **5 / 30% / +3 (committed)** | R-14, R-33, R-26, R-37, R-31 | R-14, R-33, R-26 | 0.66 |
| 3 / 30% / +3 | ≥12: the five, plus R-08, R-17, R-40, R-34, R-19, R-07, R-15 | R-14, R-33, R-26 | 0.74 |
| 10 / 30% / +3 | none (the highest share over 10 minutes is R-14's 23.7%) | ranked by share over 10: R-14, **R-35**, R-33 | — |
| 5 / 25% / +3 | the five + R-17 | R-14, R-33, R-26 | unchanged |
| 5 / 35% / +3 | R-14, R-33, R-26, R-37 (R-31 drops out) | R-14, R-33, R-26 | unchanged |
| 5 / 30% / +2 or +4 | the five, unchanged | R-14, R-33, R-26 | unchanged |

For the 3-minute row I listed only the routes the tool returned; routes ranked below #14 weren't enumerated.

- **Stable everywhere tested:** R-14 at #1 and R-33 at #2, and R-26 at #3 across tolerances 3–5, shares 25–35% and median floors 2–4.
- **The 10-minute row is a different question.** The 30% share was set for a 5-minute definition. A 10-minute tolerance measures severe lateness, where R-35's disruption naturally dominates, and R-37 and R-17 (4.8%) edge past R-26 (3.9%).
- **Marginal:** R-31 drops out at 35%, and R-17 comes in at 25% or a 3-minute tolerance.

## 7. "Why should I trust this when reasonable assumptions change the ranking?"
The strongest honest answer:

> Don't trust it because it can't move. Trust it because we've shown exactly what moves it. The rules were fixed before we saw the ranking and haven't been tuned. Every number can be traced to individual trips. Within any reasonable 5-minute-style definition (tolerance 3–5, share threshold 25–35%, median floor 2–4), the top two never change, R-26 stays third, and the LATE core of R-14, R-33, R-26 and R-37 holds; only the two routes we already call marginal move. Data errors can't change any verdict even in the worst case. Two things genuinely change the answer, and we name them: (1) applying REC-114 to every trip on R-14 and R-27, which the data can't support and which contradicts the "no change" note on R-27, and for which we give the full reconciliation; and (2) redefining "worst" as severe lateness, which is a different question, answered by our R-35 disruption finding. Our third place is a statistical near-tie with R-37, and we say so rather than hide it.

## Recommendations for the decision record
I'll draft these only once you approve.
1. Keep D8 and D10 unchanged.
2. Present #3 as "R-26 (close call over R-37)", and recommend joint follow-up on both.
3. Mark R-31 and R-17 as marginal, with their trip margins.
4. Give R-35 its own "worst single-day disruption" section, not a line in the NOT LATE list.
5. Put REC-114 in the main body with the counterfactual worst-three, worded as "applied; zero identifiable trips".
6. Include the data-quality worst-case bound as one sentence plus the table above.

content.content:
# Cityflo — AI Engineer take-home

You are helping **Priya**, an Ops Lead, answer one question for a Friday review: *which routes were
actually late this week, by how much, and which three were worst* — as a verdict she can defend when
people who lose money by it start poking holes.

Read `HANDOFF.md`. You have the week's GPS export and an ops log. You'll build a small MCP server your
agent drives to answer Priya's question, and you'll hand back **the decision, not just the tool.**

**Timebox: 4–6 focused hours.** Use whatever AI tooling you normally use — that's the point; see below.

---

## What's in the bundle

- `HANDOFF.md` — Priya's ask, in her words, including two signed-off ops directives.
- `trips.csv` — ~5,000 GPS-derived trip rows, ~40 routes, this week. Columns are documented in
  `DATA_GUIDE.md`. It's real-shaped data: some of it is wrong.
- `schedule_v2.csv` — the revised timetable REC-114 refers to (see HANDOFF).
- `ops_log.txt` — free-text ops chatter from the week.

## What to build

A small MCP server your agent can call to answer Priya's question. Wire it into your agent and actually
use it — we want to see the tool driven, not just written. Note up front: the naive answer here is a

"""Directive (a): no rider phone numbers or verbatim complaint text in any tool output."""
import re

_PATTERNS = [
    re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+"),                                   # e-mail
    re.compile(r"(?<![\w-])(?:\+?91[\s-]?)?[6-9]\d{4}[\s-]?\d{5}(?![\w-])"),   # Indian mobile
    re.compile(r"(?<![\w-])0\d{2,4}[\s-]?\d{6,8}(?![\w-])"),                    # landline with STD code
    re.compile(r"\d{10,}"),                                                     # any long digit run
]
MASK = "[REDACTED]"


def redact_text(s: str) -> str:
    for p in _PATTERNS:
        s = p.sub(MASK, s)
    return s


def redact(obj):
    """Recursively redact every string in a tool result."""
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        return redact_text(obj)
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        return {k: redact(v) for k, v in obj.items()}
    if isinstance(obj, (list, tuple)):
        return [redact(v) for v in obj]
    return obj

content.content:
I've finished discovery and haven't built anything. The bundle is in `bundle/`, and my exploration scripts are in the scratchpad, outside the repo. One thing first: the files include a **BRIEF.md** that wasn't in my earlier summary of the assignment. It's the actual grading spec, so section A is based on it.

## A. Exact deliverables
1. **MCP server** plus a short note on how to run it. A working server that parses the data is assumed, not credited. They don't score polish, test count or framework choice.
2. **`DECISION.md`**: one verdict per route (a table is fine). For the worst-three and every borderline call, it needs four things:
   - **Rule:** stated so a stranger could re-run it on next week's data and get the same answer.
   - **Case it breaks on:** the specific trip or route id where the rule gives an answer you'd argue against, and why you keep the rule anyway.
   - **Cost and who pays:** in Priya's terms (the depot head's incentive, the rider refund queue), sized from our own numbers.
   - **What would change your mind.**

   A balanced memo that hands the choice back to Priya "scores near zero."
3. **`decisions.jsonl`**: `{"decision","quote","anchor"}`. The quote must be your verbatim message and the anchor must point to it in the transcript. Unanchored entries aren't read. Honesty counts ("agent proposed X, I kept it because Y"). There's no minimum count.
4. **Raw session transcript**, exported. A reconstruction caps the score.
5. **Submission**: a public repo or gist, then `get_session_log_upload_url` and `submit_assignment`. Those two tools come from the careers MCP connector you used last session, and they aren't loaded here. We'll need that connector at submit time.

## B. Not required
- **No UI.** Priya's "something I can click into" is met by drill-down MCP tools.
- No cloud, database, test suite, polished README or framework choice.
- No LLM calls inside the server. The agent driving it is Claude Code itself.

## C. Data-quality findings
`trips.csv` has 5,292 rows, 40 routes, 105–154 trips per route. It covers Mon 2026-08-03 to Sun 08-09, 06:00–21:55, and every route runs the same number of trips each day. There are no exact duplicates and no dropped columns.

| Issue | Rows | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| `actual_arrival = "…08:60"` | 24 | Impossible time, always exactly `08:60` whatever the departure time. A device sentinel; 14 of the 24 are on Sunday. |
| Arrival exactly 5 min **before** scheduled departure | 18 | Lateness of −40 to −60. A systematic device artifact on 17 routes. Kept in, these would make routes look *better*. |
| `tz_offset +00:00` | 1 | T1-02864 (R-23), stamped in UTC. Converted to IST it's −2 min, a normal trip. |
| R-35 on Wed 08-05 | 19 | **Every** R-35 trip that day was 36–61 min late, all day. R-35's other six days have a median of +1. |
| `vehicle_series` | all | Two digits, always equal to the route number (R-14 → "14"). **No row can be identified as "4xx".** |

What survives cleaning is very clean. 5,250 trips remain, the network median is +2 min and p95 is +9. Each trip's scheduled runtime genuinely predicts its actual runtime (correlation 0.80): a 35-min slot averages 36.8 min actual and a 55-min slot averages 56.9.

**Ops log traps:**
- HANDOFF calls it **"last week's ops log"**, while DATA_GUIDE says "from the week". It has weekdays only, no dates, and doesn't join to the trips.
- Its Wednesday entry says western corridor, about 35 min, AM only. R-35's Wednesday was about 52 min and lasted all day, so it doesn't match.

**PII:** there are no phone numbers or complaint text in this bundle ("[REDACTED]" is already just a category). The debrief's fresh data might include some, so the server should redact anyway.

### The big one: REC-114
`schedule_v2` sets a single flat runtime per route, R-14 → 53 and R-27 → 45 ("no change"), effective 08-05.

| | Export timetable | REC-114 applied all week | REC-114 from 08-05 only |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-14 median / % trips >5 min late | **+8 / 72%** | **0 / 31%** | +4 / 43% |
| R-27 median / % trips >5 min late | +2 / 22% | **+5 / 47%** | +4 / 43% |

- **It clears the worst route.** R-14 is late at *every* runtime level: about +8 whether the slot is 35 or 55 minutes. A flat 53 marks a 35-min slot that took 43 as "10 min early." That isn't measuring lateness; it's moving the goalposts so "the numbers line up with what the review already has."
- **It pushes an ordinary route up.** For R-27, "no change" is false: the flat 45 changes the target for about 80% of its trips.
- **It can't be applied as written.** No trip in the data can be identified as 4xx.

## D. Consequential decisions for you
- **D1. Definition of "late."**
  - Options: (a) arrival vs timetable, `actual_arrival − (scheduled_departure + scheduled_runtime_min)`; (b) actual runtime vs the route's typical runtime.
  - Data: the per-trip timetable is accurate. Option (b) measures variability, not lateness. We have no actual departure time, so a late start can't be separated from slow running.
  - Recommendation: **(a)**.
  - Risk: a depot head argues the bus left late because of a yard problem. We can't split that out.
  - Would change it: actual departure timestamps.
- **D2. REC-114.**
  - Options: (a) apply literally all week; (b) apply from 08-05; (c) don't let it drive the verdict, but show a REC-114 column side by side and explain why; (d) apply to the trips identifiable as 4xx, which is zero.
  - Recommendation: **(c)**, stated as a deliberate decision not to apply it to the verdict.
  - Risk: you're seen overriding a signed-off directive, and regional's numbers won't match. The directive does say "apply them as you see fit."
  - Would change it: a vehicle register mapping series to 4xx, **plus** evidence that riders were told the revised times from 08-05, so refund eligibility is legitimately measured against them.
- **D3. The `08:60` rows.** Recommendation: exclude and list them. They can't be repaired.

from ontime import server as S

    json.dumps(out)  # every tool result must be JSON-serialisable

    counts = t["status"].value_counts().to_dict()
    assert counts["invalid_arrival"] == 24                      # D3: every 08:60 row
    assert counts["arrival_not_after_departure"] == 18          # D4
    assert counts["valid"] == 5250
    row = t[t.trip_id == "T1-02864"].iloc[0]                    # D5: UTC row kept, converted
    assert row.status == "valid" and "tz_corrected" in row["flags"] and row.lateness_min == -2


def test_rec114_not_applied_without_identifiable_4xx():
    t = A.load(WEEK)["trips"]
    assert not t["is_4xx"].any()
    assert (t.loc[t.status == "valid", "runtime_source"] == "export").all()
    dq = call("data_quality_report", dataset=WEEK)
    assert dq["rec114_identifiability"]["issue"].startswith("DATA-QUALITY ISSUE")


def test_independent_recompute_matches_tool():
    """Recompute verdicts and ranking from the raw CSV with a separate, minimal code path."""
    d = pd.read_csv(RAW, dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)
    dep = pd.to_datetime(d.scheduled_departure, format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", errors="coerce")
    arr = pd.to_datetime(d.actual_arrival, format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", errors="coerce")
    off = d.tz_offset.str.extract(r"([+-])(\d\d):(\d\d)")
    off_min = (off[1].astype(float) * 60 + off[2].astype(float)) * np.where(off[0] == "-", -1, 1)
    arr = arr - pd.to_timedelta(off_min, unit="min") + pd.Timedelta(minutes=330)
    late = (arr - dep).dt.total_seconds() / 60 - d.scheduled_runtime_min.astype(float)
    ok = arr.notna() & (arr > dep)
    g = pd.DataFrame({"route": d.route[ok], "late": late[ok]}).groupby("route").late
    share, med = g.apply(lambda x: (x > 5).mean()), g.median()
    expected_late = sorted(r for r in share.index if share[r] >= 0.30 and med[r] >= 3)

    v = call("route_verdicts", dataset=WEEK)
    w = call("worst_routes", dataset=WEEK)
    assert sorted(v["late_routes"]) == expected_late

# DECISION — which routes were late, week of 3–9 Aug 2026

For Priya, Friday review. Every number here comes from the `cityflo-ontime` MCP server (dataset
`week-2026-08-03`, committed defaults, `what_if: false` unless stated otherwise). Each one can be
traced to individual trips with the `trips` and `route_detail` tools. The rules are in [SPEC.md](SPEC.md).

## 1. Verdict

**Five routes were late this week, and all five were systematically late, not one bad day.**

| Rank | Route | Trips >5 min late | Median | p95 | Days the rule passes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **R-14** | 85 / 118 (72.0%) | +8 | +16 | 7/7 |
| **2** | **R-33** | 49 / 104 (47.1%) | +5 | +11 | 7/7 |
| **3** | **R-26** | 44 / 103 (42.7%) | +4 | +10 | 5/7 |
| 4 | R-37 | 42 / 105 (40.0%) | +4 | +10 | 6/7 |
| 5 | R-31 | 37 / 112 (33.0%) | +4 | +9 | 4/7 |

- **The worst three are R-14, R-33 and R-26.** R-14 and R-33 are clear calls. **R-26 vs R-37 is a
  close call (§3.2).** We rank R-26 third under the committed rule and recommend **joint operational
  follow-up on R-26 and R-37**.
- **The LATE line is marginal at both edges.** R-31 is LATE with 3 late trips to spare. R-17 is NOT
  LATE, 4 late trips short of the line (§3.3).
- **R-35 is not systematically late, but it had the week's worst single-day disruption.** On Wed 5 Aug
  all 19 trips were 36–61 min late, giving 880 excess rider-minutes (§3.4).
- **REC-114 is applied to every trip the data identifies as 4xx. This week's export identifies zero
  such trips.** If REC-114 were instead applied to whole routes, the worst three would change (§4).
- **Data quality:** 5,292 rows, 5,250 valid, 42 excluded. Even under the worst-case treatment of the
  excluded rows, no verdict and no worst-three position changes (§5).

## 2. The rules (re-runnable on next week's data)

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| D1 | `lateness = actual_arrival (in IST) − (scheduled_departure + applicable runtime)`, in minutes. |
| D2 | The applicable runtime is the export's `scheduled_runtime_min`. The exception is a trip that is **identifiably 4xx** (`vehicle_series`/class is exactly `4NN`) on or after `schedule_v2.effective_date`: that trip uses `revised_runtime_min`. The REC-114 impact is always shown separately. |
| D3 | An unparseable `actual_arrival` (e.g. `08:60`) is excluded and listed by trip id. It is never repaired. |
| D4 | An arrival not after the scheduled departure is excluded from the lateness calculation and stays visible in the data-quality output. |
| D5 | Each arrival is converted from its stamped `tz_offset` to +05:30 and kept. A missing offset excludes the trip `[impl]`. |
| D6 | The ops log is context only. Its entries have no date, so it never excludes, adjusts or excuses a trip. |
| D7 | A trip is **late** when lateness is > 5 min. |
| D8 | A route is **LATE** when ≥ 30% of its valid trips are > 5 min late **and** its median lateness is ≥ +3 min, computed on all valid trips. Otherwise it is **NOT LATE**. |
| D9 | Incident days are **never removed** from D8. A route-day whose median lateness is > 15 min is an incident day `[impl]`. A LATE route is labelled *systematic* (no incident days), *mixed* (still LATE without them) or *incident_driven* (LATE only because of them). A NOT LATE route that has an incident day is labelled *incident_day_only*. |
| D10 | Worst-N is ranked by late share (descending), then median (descending), then route code (ascending). Day-bootstrap rank stability (1,000 seeded draws) is reported as supporting evidence. |
| D11 | Rider impact (late trips; excess minutes = Σ max(0, lateness − 5)) is reported separately and never drives the ranking. |

Re-run: `route_verdicts`, then `worst_routes`, `route_detail <route>`, `data_quality_report` and
`rec114_impact`, all on the new dataset folder.

## 3. Consequential calls

### 3.1 Worst #1 R-14 and #2 R-33
- **Rule:** D10 on D8-valid trips.
- **Where it could break:**
  - R-14 is #1 only under the export timetable. If REC-114 were applied to every R-14 trip, it would
    fall to #3 or out of LATE altogether (§4).
  - A mean-lateness ranking would put R-35 (+8.05) level with R-14 (+8.07), purely because of one day.
  - We keep D10 because the export timetable is the only runtime the data can support. The mean is the
    floor the brief warns about.
- **Robustness:**
  - Late every day: 7/7 days pass for both routes.
  - Bootstrap probability of a top-three finish: 1.00 for R-14, 0.94 for R-33.
  - R-14 vs R-33 is a real gap: 72.0% vs 47.1%, z ≈ 3.8 (arithmetic on the tool's counts).
- **Cost / who pays:** the R-14 and R-33 depot heads carry the "worst" label. Their riders absorbed 85
  and 49 late trips, and 416 and 182 excess minutes.
- **What would change it:** a reliable 4xx vehicle mapping that places R-14 trips on the revised
  timetable; or evidence that R-14's export runtimes are wrong. R-14 runs about +7 to +8.5 late in
  *every* runtime band from 35 to 55 min, so it is uniformly slow, not mis-scheduled for one slot.

### 3.2 Worst #3: R-26 over R-37, a close call
- **Rule:** D10. R-26 is late on 42.7% of trips against 40.0% for R-37. Both medians are +4, so the
  median doesn't separate them.
- **Where it breaks:** R-37 passes the rule on 6/7 days to R-26's 5/7, and has one more trip over 10
  minutes (5 vs 4). The share gap is about 3 trips: R-26 needs only 3 fewer late trips (41/103 = 39.8%)
  to fall below R-37. By arithmetic on the counts the difference is not statistically meaningful
  (z ≈ 0.4, p ≈ 0.7). Bootstrap probability of a top-three finish is 0.66 for R-26 and 0.29 for R-37.
- **Why we keep R-26 third:** every other measure is level or favours R-26.
  - **Day by day,** R-26 has the higher late share on 5 of 7 days. R-37 is higher on 1, and 1 is tied.
  - **R-37's extra passing days are fragile.** It passes on Sat and Sun at exactly 33.3% (5 of 15
    trips), so a single trip flips each one.
  - **Magnitude:** R-26's mean is higher (+4.51 vs +4.13), as are its excess minutes (131 vs 125) and
    late minutes (482 vs 474). The p85 and p95 are identical.
  - **Evening peak (16–20):** R-26 is 55.6% late at +7, against 26.9% at +3 for R-37. R-37's worst
    time bands are before 07:00 and after 20:00, with 10–11 trips each.
  - **Other settings:** R-26 stays third at a 3-minute tolerance, at share thresholds from 25% to 35%,
    at median floors from +2 to +4, and under the worst-case data-quality bound.
- **Cost / who pays:** R-26's depot head takes the "worst three" label on a ~3-trip margin. If follow-up
  covered only the top three, R-37's 42 late trips and 125 excess minutes would get no attention, so
  **we recommend joint follow-up on R-26 and R-37.**
- **What would change it:**
  - 3 of R-26's late trips are shown to be data errors.
  - Ridership data shows R-37's late trips carried more riders.
  - A 4xx mapping changes either route's runtimes.
  - "Worst" is redefined as severe (>10 min) lateness. On that measure R-37 is 4.8% and R-26 3.9%.

  The excluded rows cannot cause the switch (§5).

### 3.3 The LATE line: R-31 is LATE, R-17 is NOT LATE (both marginal)

| | R-31 | R-17 |
|---|---|---|
| Valid trips | 112 | 147 |
| Late (>5) | 37 (33.0%) | 41 (27.9%) |
| Median | +4 | +3 |
| Trips >10 min | 0 | 7 |
| Excess minutes | 91 | 130 |
| Days the rule passes | 4/7 | 2/7 |
| Margin to the 30% line | needs ≥34; 3 trips spare, flips at 4 fewer | needs ≥45; 4 trips short |

- **Rule:** D8 as written. The thresholds were not tuned.
- **Where it breaks:** R-17 has more late trips and more excess minutes than R-31, yet it is NOT LATE.
  - The totals are larger because R-17 runs 31% more trips. Per trip, excess lateness is about the
    same: 0.88 min vs 0.81.
  - D8 is built to flag routes that are *routinely* late. R-31 runs a steady +4 with no trip over 10
    minutes. R-17's lateness is lumpy: 52% of trips late on Friday, 14–33% on the other days.
- **Cost / who pays:**
  - A false LATE on R-31 costs its depot head the incentive on a 3-trip margin.
  - A false clear on R-17 leaves its riders' 41 late trips (130 excess minutes) out of the
    chronic-lateness list. They are still counted trip by trip in rider impact (D11), so the route
    verdict alone should never deny a refund.
- **What would change it:**
  - 4 of R-31's late trips are shown to be errors, which would make it NOT LATE.
  - 4 more of R-17's trips are confirmed late, which would make it LATE.
  - The stability check also changes the result: at a 35% share R-31 drops out; at 25%, or a 3-minute
    tolerance, R-17 comes in.

### 3.4 R-35: NOT LATE as a route, but the week's worst single disruption
> **R-35: not late as a route, but the week's worst single disruption.** On Wednesday 5 August every one
> of R-35's 19 trips ran 36–61 minutes late (median +52). That's 880 rider-minutes beyond tolerance,
> more than double R-14's whole week. Wednesday is included in R-35's verdict, not removed. The route is
> NOT LATE because the other six days ran on time (11.5% of trips late, median +1), so this looks like a
> one-day disruption, not a timetable problem. The cause is not established: no dated incident record
> was supplied, and the ops log is undated. R-35 needs an incident review and rider remediation for
> Wednesday, separate from the chronic-lateness list.

| Lens | R-35 |
|---|---|
| Rider experience this week | Bad. Wednesday was the network's worst route-day. Mean +8.05, level with R-14. |
| Systematic route lateness (D8, Wednesday **included**) | NOT LATE: 32/132 late (24.2%), median +2. 1/7 days pass. |
| Incident-driven (D9) | `incident_day_only`: Wed 5 Aug, 19/19 trips late, +36 to +61. |
| Rider impact (D11) | **#1 on the network**: 914 excess minutes, 880 of them on Wednesday. R-14 is #2 with 416. |

- **Rule:** D8 on all valid trips (D9: nothing is removed). Impact is reported under D11.
- **Where it breaks:** on a mean, or on a >10-minute measure, R-35 is #2 on the network. We keep the
  rule because the question for the worst-three is whether a route is chronically late. One day of
  disruption is a different problem with a different fix, and we report it in full here.
- **Cost / who pays:**
  - The riders on those 19 Wednesday trips are owed remediation (880 excess minutes).
  - If the disruption had a cause the depot controlled, the depot avoids a LATE label.
- **What would change it:**
  - A dated incident record showing a recurring, depot-controlled cause.
  - Further disruption days on R-35 in later weeks, which would make it systematic.

  R-35's verdict does not hinge on the 15-minute incident threshold. Its Wednesday median is +52 and its
  next-worst day is +2.

## 4. REC-114 (directive b)
HANDOFF: *"trips on the 4xx vehicle series are measured against the revised timetable in
`schedule_v2.csv` … so the numbers line up with what the review already has."*

**What we did:** REC-114 is applied, automatically, to every trip the data identifies as 4xx. **This
week's export identifies zero such trips**, so the primary result uses the export timetable everywhere.
- DATA_GUIDE defines `vehicle_series` as the *last two digits* of the vehicle class, so the field
  cannot tell 114 from 414.
- In the trips we checked, the series equals the route number: R-14 → "14", R-27 → "27", and all R-26
  trips → "26".
- `data_quality_report` raises this as an explicit data-quality issue.

**What applying it to whole routes would do (counterfactual, not the verdict).** Source: `rec114_impact`.
The re-rankings are arithmetic on its outputs.

| View | R-14 | R-27 | Worst three |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary: data-supported, 0 trips revised** | 72.0% late, +8, LATE | 22.4%, +2, NOT LATE | **R-14, R-33, R-26** |
| Counterfactual: revised runtime for every trip from 5 Aug | 43.2%, +4, LATE | 43.4%, +4, LATE | R-33, R-27, R-14 |
| Counterfactual: revised runtime for every trip all week | 31.4%, 0, NOT LATE | 46.9%, +5, LATE | R-33, R-27, R-26 |

**Why the primary result does not apply REC-114 to whole routes:**
- **The directive is defined by vehicle, not by route.** `schedule_v2` lists which routes have a
  revised timetable. It does not say which trips ran on 4xx vehicles.
- **Applying it to every trip contradicts `schedule_v2`.** The file marks R-27 *"no change"*, yet a flat
  45-minute runtime applied to all of R-27 would move it from NOT LATE into the worst three.
- **It would turn late trips into early ones.** Trip **T1-01730** (R-14, Thu 6 Aug) took 48 minutes
  against a 35-minute slot, so it is +13 late. Against a flat 53 minutes it would count as 5 minutes
  early. Across R-14's 35-minute band the average would read 9.8 minutes "early".

# DECISION — which routes were late, week of 3–9 Aug 2026

For Priya, Friday review. Every number here comes from the `cityflo-ontime` MCP server (dataset
`week-2026-08-03`, committed defaults, `what_if: false` unless stated otherwise). Each one can be
traced to individual trips with the `trips` and `route_detail` tools. The rules are in [SPEC.md](SPEC.md).

## 1. Verdict

**Five routes were late this week, and all five were systematically late, not one bad day.**

| Rank | Route | Trips >5 min late | Median | p95 | Days the rule passes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **R-14** | 85 / 118 (72.0%) | +8 | +16 | 7/7 |
| **2** | **R-33** | 49 / 104 (47.1%) | +5 | +11 | 7/7 |
| **3** | **R-26** | 44 / 103 (42.7%) | +4 | +10 | 5/7 |
| 4 | R-37 | 42 / 105 (40.0%) | +4 | +10 | 6/7 |
| 5 | R-31 | 37 / 112 (33.0%) | +4 | +9 | 4/7 |

- **The worst three are R-14, R-33 and R-26.** R-14 and R-33 are clear calls. **R-26 vs R-37 is a
  close call (§3.2).** We rank R-26 third under the committed rule and recommend **joint operational
  follow-up on R-26 and R-37**.
- **The LATE line is marginal at both edges.** R-31 is LATE with 3 late trips to spare. R-17 is NOT
  LATE, 4 late trips short of the line (§3.3).
- **R-35 is not systematically late, but it had the week's worst single-day disruption.** On Wed 5 Aug
  all 19 trips were 36–61 min late, giving 880 excess rider-minutes (§3.4).
- **REC-114 is applied to every trip the data identifies as 4xx. This week's export identifies zero
  such trips.** If REC-114 were instead applied to whole routes, the worst three would change (§4).
- **Data quality:** 5,292 rows, 5,250 valid, 42 excluded. Even under the worst-case treatment of the
  excluded rows, no verdict and no worst-three position changes (§5).

## 2. The rules (re-runnable on next week's data)

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| D1 | `lateness = actual_arrival (in IST) − (scheduled_departure + applicable runtime)`, in minutes. |
| D2 | The applicable runtime is the export's `scheduled_runtime_min`. The exception is a trip that is **identifiably 4xx** (`vehicle_series`/class is exactly `4NN`) on or after `schedule_v2.effective_date`: that trip uses `revised_runtime_min`. The REC-114 impact is always shown separately. |
| D3 | An unparseable `actual_arrival` (e.g. `08:60`) is excluded and listed by trip id. It is never repaired. |
| D4 | An arrival not after the scheduled departure is excluded from the lateness calculation and stays visible in the data-quality output. |
| D5 | Each arrival is converted from its stamped `tz_offset` to +05:30 and kept. A missing offset excludes the trip `[impl]`. |
| D6 | The ops log is context only. Its entries have no date, so it never excludes, adjusts or excuses a trip. |
| D7 | A trip is **late** when lateness is > 5 min. |
| D8 | A route is **LATE** when ≥ 30% of its valid trips are > 5 min late **and** its median lateness is ≥ +3 min, computed on all valid trips. Otherwise it is **NOT LATE**. |
| D9 | Incident days are **never removed** from D8. A route-day whose median lateness is > 15 min is an incident day `[impl]`. A LATE route is labelled *systematic* (no incident days), *mixed* (still LATE without them) or *incident_driven* (LATE only because of them). A NOT LATE route that has an incident day is labelled *incident_day_only*. |
| D10 | Worst-N is ranked by late share (descending), then median (descending), then route code (ascending). Day-bootstrap rank stability (1,000 seeded draws) is reported as supporting evidence. |
| D11 | Rider impact (late trips; excess minutes = Σ max(0, lateness − 5)) is reported separately and never drives the ranking. |

Re-run: `route_verdicts`, then `worst_routes`, `route_detail <route>`, `data_quality_report` and
`rec114_impact`, all on the new dataset folder.

## 3. Consequential calls

### 3.1 Worst #1 R-14 and #2 R-33
- **Rule:** D10 on D8-valid trips.
- **Where it could break:**
  - R-14 is #1 only under the export timetable. If REC-114 were applied to every R-14 trip, it would
    fall to #3 or out of LATE altogether (§4).
  - A mean-lateness ranking would put R-35 (+8.05) level with R-14 (+8.07), purely because of one day.
  - We keep D10 because the export timetable is the only runtime the data can support. The mean is the
    floor the brief warns about.
- **Robustness:**
  - Late every day: 7/7 days pass for both routes.
  - Bootstrap probability of a top-three finish: 1.00 for R-14, 0.94 for R-33.
  - R-14 vs R-33 is a real gap: 72.0% vs 47.1%, z ≈ 3.8 (arithmetic on the tool's counts).
- **Cost / who pays:** the R-14 and R-33 depot heads carry the "worst" label. Their riders absorbed 85
  and 49 late trips, and 416 and 182 excess minutes.
- **What would change it:** a reliable 4xx vehicle mapping that places R-14 trips on the revised
  timetable; or evidence that R-14's export runtimes are wrong. R-14 runs about +7 to +8.5 late in
  *every* runtime band from 35 to 55 min, so it is uniformly slow, not mis-scheduled for one slot.

  median doesn't separate them.

    trips), so a single trip flips each one.

    time bands are before 07:00 and after 20:00, with 10–11 trips each.

|---|---|---|

  - The totals are larger because R-17 runs 31% more trips. Per trip, excess lateness is about the
    same: 0.88 min vs 0.81.

  such trips.** If REC-114 were instead applied to whole routes, the worst three would change (§4).
- **Data quality:** 5,292 rows, 5,250 valid, 42 excluded. Even under the worst-case treatment of the
  excluded rows, no verdict and no worst-three position changes (§5).

## 2. The rules (re-runnable on next week's data)

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| D1 | `lateness = actual_arrival (in IST) − (scheduled_departure + applicable runtime)`, in minutes. |
| D2 | The applicable runtime is the export's `scheduled_runtime_min`. The exception is a trip that is **identifiably 4xx** (`vehicle_series`/class is exactly `4NN`) on or after `schedule_v2.effective_date`: that trip uses `revised_runtime_min`. The REC-114 impact is always shown separately. |
| D3 | An unparseable `actual_arrival` (e.g. `08:60`) is excluded and listed by trip id. It is never repaired. |
| D4 | An arrival not after the scheduled departure is excluded from the lateness calculation and stays visible in the data-quality output. |
| D5 | Each arrival is converted from its stamped `tz_offset` to +05:30 and kept. A missing offset excludes the trip `[impl]`. |
| D6 | The ops log is context only. Its entries have no date, so it never excludes, adjusts or excuses a trip. |
| D7 | A trip is **late** when lateness is > 5 min. |
| D8 | A route is **LATE** when ≥ 30% of its valid trips are > 5 min late **and** its median lateness is ≥ +3 min, computed on all valid trips. Otherwise it is **NOT LATE**. |
| D9 | Incident days are **never removed** from D8. A route-day whose median lateness is > 15 min is an incident day `[impl]`. A LATE route is labelled *systematic* (no incident days), *mixed* (still LATE without them) or *incident_driven* (LATE only because of them). A NOT LATE route that has an incident day is labelled *incident_day_only*. |
| D10 | Worst-N is ranked by late share (descending), then median (descending), then route code (ascending). Day-bootstrap rank stability (1,000 seeded draws) is reported as supporting evidence. |
| D11 | Rider impact (late trips; excess minutes = Σ max(0, lateness − 5)) is reported separately and never drives the ranking. |

Re-run: `route_verdicts`, then `worst_routes`, `route_detail <route>`, `data_quality_report` and
`rec114_impact`, all on the new dataset folder.

## 3. Consequential calls

### 3.1 Worst #1 R-14 and #2 R-33
- **Rule:** D10 on D8-valid trips.
- **Where it could break:**
  - R-14 is #1 only under the export timetable. If REC-114 were applied to every R-14 trip, it would
    fall to #3 or out of LATE altogether (§4).
  - A mean-lateness ranking would put R-35 (+8.05) level with R-14 (+8.07), purely because of one day.
  - We keep D10 because the export timetable is the only runtime the data can support. The mean is the
    floor the brief warns about.
- **Robustness:**
  - Late every day: 7/7 days pass for both routes.
  - Bootstrap probability of a top-three finish: 1.00 for R-14, 0.94 for R-33.
  - R-14 vs R-33 is a real gap: 72.0% vs 47.1%, z ≈ 3.8 (arithmetic on the tool's counts).
- **Cost / who pays:** the R-14 and R-33 depot heads carry the "worst" label. Their riders absorbed 85
  and 49 late trips, and 416 and 182 excess minutes.
- **What would change it:** a reliable 4xx vehicle mapping that places R-14 trips on the revised
  timetable; or evidence that R-14's export runtimes are wrong. R-14 runs about +7 to +8.5 late in
  *every* runtime band from 35 to 55 min, so it is uniformly slow, not mis-scheduled for one slot.

### 3.2 Worst #3: R-26 over R-37, a close call
- **Rule:** D10. R-26 is late on 42.7% of trips against 40.0% for R-37. Both medians are +4, so the
  median doesn't separate them.
- **Where it breaks:** R-37 passes the rule on 6/7 days to R-26's 5/7, and has one more trip over 10
  minutes (5 vs 4). The share gap is about 3 trips: R-26 needs only 3 fewer late trips (41/103 = 39.8%)
  to fall below R-37. By arithmetic on the counts the difference is not statistically meaningful
  (z ≈ 0.4, p ≈ 0.7). Bootstrap probability of a top-three finish is 0.66 for R-26 and 0.29 for R-37.
- **Why we keep R-26 third:** every other measure is level or favours R-26.
  - **Day by day,** R-26 has the higher late share on 5 of 7 days. R-37 is higher on 1, and 1 is tied.
  - **R-37's extra passing days are fragile.** It passes on Sat and Sun at exactly 33.3% (5 of 15
    trips), so a single trip flips each one.
  - **Magnitude:** R-26's mean is higher (+4.51 vs +4.13), as are its excess minutes (131 vs 125) and
    late minutes (482 vs 474). The p85 and p95 are identical.
  - **Evening peak (16–20):** R-26 is 55.6% late at +7, against 26.9% at +3 for R-37. R-37's worst
    time bands are before 07:00 and after 20:00, with 10–11 trips each.
  - **Other settings:** R-26 stays third at a 3-minute tolerance, at share thresholds from 25% to 35%,
    at median floors from +2 to +4, and under the worst-case data-quality bound.
- **Cost / who pays:** R-26's depot head takes the "worst three" label on a ~3-trip margin. If follow-up
  covered only the top three, R-37's 42 late trips and 125 excess minutes would get no attention, so
  **we recommend joint follow-up on R-26 and R-37.**
- **What would change it:**
  - 3 of R-26's late trips are shown to be data errors.
  - Ridership data shows R-37's late trips carried more riders.
  - A 4xx mapping changes either route's runtimes.
  - "Worst" is redefined as severe (>10 min) lateness. On that measure R-37 is 4.8% and R-26 3.9%.

  The excluded rows cannot cause the switch (§5).

### 3.3 The LATE line: R-31 is LATE, R-17 is NOT LATE (both marginal)

| | R-31 | R-17 |
|---|---|---|
| Valid trips | 112 | 147 |
| Late (>5) | 37 (33.0%) | 41 (27.9%) |
| Median | +4 | +3 |
| Trips >10 min | 0 | 7 |
| Excess minutes | 91 | 130 |
| Days the rule passes | 4/7 | 2/7 |
| Margin to the 30% line | needs ≥34; 3 trips spare, flips at 4 fewer | needs ≥45; 4 trips short |

- **Rule:** D8 as written. The thresholds were not tuned.
- **Where it breaks:** R-17 has more late trips and more excess minutes than R-31, yet it is NOT LATE.
  - The totals are larger because R-17 runs 31% more trips. Per trip, excess lateness is about the
    same: 0.88 min vs 0.81.
  - D8 is built to flag routes that are *routinely* late. R-31 runs a steady +4 with no trip over 10
    minutes. R-17's lateness is lumpy: 52% of trips late on Friday, 14–33% on the other days.
- **Cost / who pays:**
  - A false LATE on R-31 costs its depot head the incentive on a 3-trip margin.
  - A false clear on R-17 leaves its riders' 41 late trips (130 excess minutes) out of the
    chronic-lateness list. They are still counted trip by trip in rider impact (D11), so the route
    verdict alone should never deny a refund.
- **What would change it:**
  - 4 of R-31's late trips are shown to be errors, which would make it NOT LATE.
  - 4 more of R-17's trips are confirmed late, which would make it LATE.
  - The stability check also changes the result: at a 35% share R-31 drops out; at 25%, or a 3-minute
    tolerance, R-17 comes in.

### 3.4 R-35: NOT LATE as a route, but the week's worst single disruption
> **R-35: not late as a route, but the week's worst single disruption.** On Wednesday 5 August every one
> of R-35's 19 trips ran 36–61 minutes late (median +52). That's 880 rider-minutes beyond tolerance,
> more than double R-14's whole week. Wednesday is included in R-35's verdict, not removed. The route is
> NOT LATE because the other six days ran on time (11.5% of trips late, median +1), so this looks like a
> one-day disruption, not a timetable problem. The cause is not established: no dated incident record
> was supplied, and the ops log is undated. R-35 needs an incident review and rider remediation for
> Wednesday, separate from the chronic-lateness list.

| Lens | R-35 |
|---|---|
| Rider experience this week | Bad. Wednesday was the network's worst route-day. Mean +8.05, level with R-14. |
| Systematic route lateness (D8, Wednesday **included**) | NOT LATE: 32/132 late (24.2%), median +2. 1/7 days pass. |
| Incident-driven (D9) | `incident_day_only`: Wed 5 Aug, 19/19 trips late, +36 to +61. |
| Rider impact (D11) | **#1 on the network**: 914 excess minutes, 880 of them on Wednesday. R-14 is #2 with 416. |

- **Rule:** D8 on all valid trips (D9: nothing is removed). Impact is reported under D11.
- **Where it breaks:** on a mean, or on a >10-minute measure, R-35 is #2 on the network. We keep the
  rule because the question for the worst-three is whether a route is chronically late. One day of
  disruption is a different problem with a different fix, and we report it in full here.
- **Cost / who pays:**
  - The riders on those 19 Wednesday trips are owed remediation (880 excess minutes).
  - If the disruption had a cause the depot controlled, the depot avoids a LATE label.
- **What would change it:**
  - A dated incident record showing a recurring, depot-controlled cause.
  - Further disruption days on R-35 in later weeks, which would make it systematic.

  R-35's verdict does not hinge on the 15-minute incident threshold. Its Wednesday median is +52 and its
  next-worst day is +2.

## 4. REC-114 (directive b)
HANDOFF: *"trips on the 4xx vehicle series are measured against the revised timetable in
`schedule_v2.csv` … so the numbers line up with what the review already has."*

**What we did:** REC-114 is applied, automatically, to every trip the data identifies as 4xx. **This
week's export identifies zero such trips**, so the primary result uses the export timetable everywhere.
- DATA_GUIDE defines `vehicle_series` as the *last two digits* of the vehicle class, so the field
  cannot tell 114 from 414.
- In the trips we checked, the series equals the route number: R-14 → "14", R-27 → "27", and all R-26
  trips → "26".
- `data_quality_report` raises this as an explicit data-quality issue.

**What applying it to whole routes would do (counterfactual, not the verdict).** Source: `rec114_impact`.
The re-rankings are arithmetic on its outputs.

| View | R-14 | R-27 | Worst three |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary: data-supported, 0 trips revised** | 72.0% late, +8, LATE | 22.4%, +2, NOT LATE | **R-14, R-33, R-26** |
| Counterfactual: revised runtime for every trip from 5 Aug | 43.2%, +4, LATE | 43.4%, +4, LATE | R-33, R-27, R-14 |
| Counterfactual: revised runtime for every trip all week | 31.4%, 0, NOT LATE | 46.9%, +5, LATE | R-33, R-27, R-26 |

**Why the primary result does not apply REC-114 to whole routes:**
- **The directive is defined by vehicle, not by route.** `schedule_v2` lists which routes have a
  revised timetable. It does not say which trips ran on 4xx vehicles.
- **Applying it to every trip contradicts `schedule_v2`.** The file marks R-27 *"no change"*, yet a flat
  45-minute runtime applied to all of R-27 would move it from NOT LATE into the worst three.
- **It would turn late trips into early ones.** Trip **T1-01730** (R-14, Thu 6 Aug) took 48 minutes
  against a 35-minute slot, so it is +13 late. Against a flat 53 minutes it would count as 5 minutes
  early. Across R-14's 35-minute band the average would read 9.8 minutes "early".

**Rule:** apply REC-114 to identifiable 4xx trips only, and always publish the route-wide
counterfactual next to the verdict.
- **Where it breaks:** if the review's existing numbers were computed route-wide, ours will not match
  them. The table above is the reconciliation.
- **Cost / who pays:** route-wide application would relieve R-14's depot (excess minutes 416 → 249 or
  166) and penalise R-27's (104 → 384 or 447). It would drop 34 to 48 of R-14's late trips out of the
  late count.
- **What would change it:** a vehicle register or a debrief dataset with a reliable 4xx mapping. The
  server then applies the revised runtime to those trips automatically, from the effective date. No
  rule change is needed.

## 5. Data quality and the worst-case bound
| Exclusion | Rows | Evidence it is an artifact |
|---|---|---|
| `actual_arrival` = `…08:60` (D3) | 24 | It's always exactly `08:60`, whatever the departure time. |
| Arrival before scheduled departure (D4) | 18 | Every one is exactly 5 minutes before departure. |
| Missing `tz_offset` (D5) | 0 | The rule exists; nothing triggered it this week. |
| *Converted, kept:* `+00:00` offset (D5) | 1 | T1-02864 (R-23) works out to −2 min after conversion to IST. |

- **The 24 `08:60` trips:** T1-00136, 00352, 00470, 00734, 01372, 02034, 02470, 02585, 02930, 03274,
  03297, 03396, 03414, 03490, 03641, 03669, 03716, 03733, 03822, 04337, 04466, 04646, 04846, 05210.
- **The 18 pre-departure trips:** T1-00361, 00392, 00417, 00673, 01111, 01303, 01419, 01691, 02488,
  02697, 02730, 03142, 03377, 03491, 03636, 04381, 04540, 05264.
- **The most excluded from any one route is 4 (R-27).** Among the LATE routes: R-14 1, R-33 1, R-26 2,
  R-37 0, R-31 0.

**Worst-case bound.** We treated every excluded row first as extremely late, then as on time:

| Route | Excluded | Late share as reported | Range under both extremes |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-14 | 1 | 72.0% | 71.4–72.3% |
| R-33 | 1 | 47.1% | 46.7–47.6% |
| R-26 | 2 | 42.7% | 41.9–43.8% (always above R-37's fixed 40.0%) |
| R-37 / R-31 / R-17 | 0 | 40.0 / 33.0 / 27.9% | fixed |
| R-35 | 1 | 24.2% | at most 24.8% |
| R-27 | 4 | 22.4% | at most 24.5% |

**No verdict and no worst-three position changes under either extreme.** Excluding the rows is
therefore not doing the deciding. Including them would only add invented values.

## 6. Threshold sensitivity
These are what-if runs of `worst_routes` (`what_if: true`). Only the first row is the committed answer.

| Tolerance / share / median floor | LATE routes | Worst three |
|---|---|---|
| **5 / 30% / +3 (committed)** | R-14, R-33, R-26, R-37, R-31 | **R-14, R-33, R-26** |
| 3 / 30% / +3 | ≥ 12 (the five above, plus R-08, R-17, R-40, R-34, R-19, R-07, R-15) | R-14, R-33, R-26 |
| 5 / 25% / +3 | the five + R-17 | R-14, R-33, R-26 |
| 5 / 35% / +3 | R-14, R-33, R-26, R-37 (R-31 drops out) | R-14, R-33, R-26 |
| 5 / 30% / +2 and 5 / 30% / +4 | the five, unchanged | R-14, R-33, R-26 |
| 10 / 30% / +3 | none (the highest share over 10 min is R-14's 23.7%) | by share over 10 min: R-14, R-35, R-33 |

- **The worst three and the core of R-14, R-33, R-26 and R-37 hold across every 3–5-minute variant.**
  Only the two routes we already call marginal move.
- **A 10-minute tolerance asks a different question.** It measures severe lateness, where R-35's
  Wednesday naturally dominates. That is why §3.4 reports R-35 in its own right.

## 7. Why trust this when assumptions can move the ranking?
Not because the ranking can't move, but because we have shown exactly what moves it.

- **The rules were fixed before the ranking was seen,** and the thresholds were not tuned.
- **Every number traces to trip ids** through the same tools a reviewer can drive.
- **Within any reasonable 5-minute-style definition the answer holds.** Tolerance 3–5, share 25–35% and
  median floor +2 to +4 all leave the top two unchanged and R-26 third. Data errors cannot change any
  verdict, even in the worst case.
- **Two things genuinely change the answer, and both are named here:**
  1. **REC-114 applied to every trip on R-14 and R-27.** The data cannot support that, and it
     contradicts R-27's "no change" note. The full reconciliation is in §4.
  2. **Redefining "worst" as severe lateness.** That is a different question, answered by the R-35
     finding.
- **The call we are least sure of is #3, R-26 over R-37.** It is a statistical near-tie. We say so,
  commit to R-26 under the rule, and recommend acting on both.

## 8. Ops log (D6)
The ops log has six entries with a weekday but no date. HANDOFF calls it *last week's* log, while
DATA_GUIDE says it is from this week. It is shown, redacted and by category, through the `ops_log` tool,
and it never adjusts or excuses a trip.

Its Wednesday entry, a western-corridor diversion of about 35 minutes in the morning, does not match
R-35's all-day delay of +36 to +61 minutes. So it cannot be used to explain or excuse R-35.
